newsitem.title: UK: Sumitomo can happen again - metals exchange chairman.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo can happen again - metals exchange chairman.

text.p: Tightened metals trading rules and more co-operation among global regulators will never erase the possibility of scandals like the Sumitomo affair reoccurring, the chairman of the London Metal Exchange (LME) said on Thursday.
"It would be naive to believe that they cannot happen again," LME Chairman Raj Bagri told a news conference.
UK regulator the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) on Thursday urged the LME to strengthen rules and release more information after a six-month review sparked by the Sumitomo scandal.
"You can never stop people going berserk, being greedy or just plain foolish," Bagri said.
But the changes recommended by the SIB and to be implemented by the LME would lessen the chance of rogue traders running up huge losses and hiding them, he added.

Sumitomo Corp rocked the financial markets in June when it uncovered a tangled web of unauthorised trades. It sacked star copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he had confessed to running up $2.6 billion in losses.
Internal controls by trading companies were key to preventing future scandals, Bagri said.
LME Chief Executive David King told the news conference that information voluntarily provided by LME members was key to uncovering the Sumitomo scandal.
But in response to the SIB review, the LME would change its rulebook requiring LME members to provide information not only on their own business but on the business of their customers, he added.
A great deal of metals business is done off exchange, however, and that remains a sticky problem, Bagri and King said.
In addition, firms like Sumitomo can trade LME contracts through third parties and escape regulation.

"We have said many times that we find it incongruous that under current legislation it is possible to trade actively in many millions of tonnes in LME contracts in the UK without the obligation to be an LME member," Bagri said.

The LME hopes that better cooperation among international regulators will help solve the problem and is looking forward to detailed proposals from the SIB and the Securities and Futures Authority, he said.
Global regulators from 27 countries agreed in November a wide-ranging progamme to strengthen supervision in many of the world's commodity markets, but fell short of proposing any new measures.
